newsitem.title: USA: Germany has mixed feelings on high IMF lending.
newsitem.headline: Germany has mixed feelings on high IMF lending.

text.p: Germany said on Tuesday it was willing to contribute to a rise in International Monetary Fund quotas and a new stand-by loan facility, but had mixed views about the IMF's lending rising to record levels.

In a speech to the annual meeting of the IMF and World Bank annual meeting, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said, "We are viewing the rise in the IMF's lending to a record level with mixed feelings," he said.
Although it was positive that help had been offered to members in need, there was a danger of moral hazard, he said.
Tietmeyer said Germany had two main concerns about the record lending.
"Firstly, the IMF must not become a lender of last resort for certain groups of creditors who have entered into excessively large exposures and as a result reaped large risk premia," he said.
He added that bail-out operations of this kind could undermine the discipline of the international financial markets to the detriment of global stability.

"Secondly, building up undue credit exposures financed by central bank resources is problematic in terms of global anti-inflation policy and might ultimately undermine the financial integrity of the IMF," he added.
"A great appreciation of these principles, including the catalytic role of the IMF, would appear to be warranted," he continued.
Tietmeyer said that, despite these concerns, Germany was prepared to make a substantial contribution to a new stand-by facility for the IMF, the New Arrangements to Borrow.
It would also make a positive contribution within the framework of a review of IMF quotas -- the Fund's share capital.

"Germany remains willing to cooperate in the 11th quota review in a constructive manner with the view to meeting the IMF's need for liquidity as justified by its mandate," he said according to the text of a speech.

Germany remained opposed to a general allocation of Special Drawing Rights, the IMF's own currency, but would support a smaller allocation to give those countries which have never held SDRs an allocation.
